findings.failure_path: A valid narrow init followed by a widened init containing sufficiently deeply nested metadata, then a successful result, is accepted. json.loads raises RecursionError on the widened event; the existing per-line guard discards it, leaving only the narrow init in offered. Thus the check cannot establish that every init respected the boundary.
findings.smallest_fix: Track undecodable stream events and reject otherwise successful boundary-checked runs when any occur, preserving terminal-error precedence. Add a regression containing a narrow init, an undecodable widened init and success.

findings.failure_path: ignore_cleanup_errors=True allows successful answers to be returned even when the temporary directory remains. For example, an enabled hook's background process can recreate files during removal, causing ENOTEMPTY, which cleanup suppresses. This violates the removal guarantee; the tests exercise only successful cleanup.
findings.smallest_fix: Detect and report unsuccessful cleanup instead of silently accepting the run. Preserve an existing run error, and add a cleanup-failure regression verifying that retained directories cannot accompany an accepted sample.

findings.failure_path: The repeated-init case tests only narrow-then-widened. Mutating collection to retain only the latest init leaves this suite green, as well as the Ruby cases, while widened-then-narrow streams become accepted. The protected requirement to validate every init therefore lacks a killing test and mutation.
findings.smallest_fix: Add widened-then-narrow cases to both runners and record an applied mutation that retains only the latest init; those cases must fail under that mutation.

skipped_clients.reason: claude belongs to the implementer model family

concern_results.conclusion: Argv restrictions, signature versioning and residual-read documentation match the profile. Python can silently discard boundary evidence or suppress failed cleanup, and the tests miss an init-ordering regression.

challenge_focus: Try to break the tool boundary and the evidence: a way for the tested agent or judge to still run a shell, write, reach an MCP tool or read the other arm's saved answers despite --strict-mcp-config/--tools and the fresh directory; an init event shape or ordering that passes the check while more tools were offered; a resumed run that banks a sample from the old argv; temp-directory cleanup that deletes or leaks something; tests or mutations that would stay green with the defect present; and doc or register text that claims more isolation than the code gives.
